topics.title: Current, potential difference and Ohm's law

learn.hook: Electricity in a wire is like water in a pipe: the 'push' is voltage, the flow is current, and narrow pipes resist!
points: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q/t. Its SI unit is the ampere (A); 1 A = 1 coulomb per second. Conventionally current flows from + to −, opposite to the flow of electrons. It is measured by an ammeter connected in series.
Potential difference (V) between two points is the work done to move a unit charge between them: V = W/Q. Its unit is the volt; 1 V = 1 J/C. It is measured by a voltmeter connected in parallel.

Ohm's law: at constant temperature, the current through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it: V = IR. R is the resistance, measured in ohms (Ω); 1 Ω = 1 V/A.
Resistance of a uniform conductor: R = ρl/A. It increases with length (l), decreases with cross-sectional area (A) and depends on the material through its resistivity ρ (unit Ω m).

Metals like copper and aluminium have low resistivity and are used for wires; alloys like nichrome have higher resistivity and do not oxidise readily at high temperatures, so they are used in heating elements; glass and rubber are insulators.

example.q: A bulb draws a current of 0.5 A from a 220 V supply. What is the resistance of its filament?

learn.reallife: Electricians use copper wires inside your walls because copper has very low resistivity, so little energy is wasted as heat.

I = 2 A, R = 5 Ω. Voltage in V?
V = 6 V, I = 0.5 A. Resistance in Ω?

quiz.q: A current of 0.5 A flows through a lamp for 10 minutes. How much charge (in coulombs) flows?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert minutes into seconds

quiz.q: How is an ammeter connected in a circuit?
options: It is not connected at all
quiz.explain: An ammeter measures the current flowing through a component, so it is placed in series.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up ammeter and voltmeter connections

quiz.q: How much work (in joules) is done in moving a charge of 2 C across a potential difference of 12 V?
quiz.mistake: Divides instead of multiplying
steps: V = W/Q, so W = V × Q

quiz.q: What is the resistance (in ohms) of a bulb filament that draws 0.5 A from a 220 V supply?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies V and I instead of dividing

quiz.q: A wire's length is doubled while its thickness and material stay the same. Its resistance —
quiz.explain: R = ρl/A, so R is directly proportional to length.
quiz.mistake: Thinks length does not affect resistance

quiz.q: Why are heating elements made of alloys such as nichrome?
options: They have high resistivity and do not oxidise readily at high temperatures
quiz.explain: A high resistivity alloy produces more heat and does not burn (oxidise) easily when red hot.
quiz.mistake: Thinks heaters need low-resistance materials

quiz.q: Ohm's law is valid only when —
options: The wire is made of rubber
The temperature of the conductor remains constant
quiz.explain: Resistance changes with temperature, so V ∝ I holds only at constant temperature.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the condition of constant temperature

quiz.q: Two wires of the same material and length have cross-sectional areas A and 2A. Compared with the thin wire, the thick wire's resistance is —
quiz.explain: R = ρl/A, so doubling the area halves the resistance.
quiz.mistake: Thinks thicker wires have more resistance

teach.ask: Gappu sits on a wire: 'What is the difference between current and voltage? And what does Ohm's law say?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Voltage pushes charge, current is the flow, and V = IR when the temperature stays constant!
teach.nudge: Good! But how are voltage and current related in Ohm's law?

learn.hook: Why can one fused bulb in a series string of fairy lights switch off the whole string, but your house lights stay on? Series vs parallel!
points: Series: resistors joined end to end. The same current flows through each; the total voltage is shared: V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃. Equivalent resistance Rₛ = R₁ + R₂ + R₃, which is larger than any single resistor.
Parallel: resistors joined across the same two points. Each has the same potential difference; the total current divides: I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃.
Equivalent resistance in parallel: 1/Rₚ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃. Rₚ is smaller than the smallest individual resistance.
In series, if one component fails the whole circuit breaks, and all components share one current — unsuitable for appliances with different needs.
Homes use parallel wiring: each appliance gets the full mains voltage, draws its own current and can be switched on or off independently.

example.q: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel to a 6 V battery. Find the equivalent resistance and the total current.
steps: Check: 6 Ω carries 1 A and 3 Ω carries 2 A; 1 + 2 = 3 A.

learn.reallife: If the fridge is switched off, the TV keeps working — because every socket in your home is connected in parallel.

games.title: Circuit check
items: In a series circuit, the current is the same in every part.
There is only one path for charge to flow.
The equivalent resistance of resistors in parallel is greater than the largest resistor.
It is less than the smallest resistor.
In parallel, each resistor has the same potential difference across it.
All are connected across the same two points.
Household appliances are connected in series.
They are connected in parallel so each gets full voltage and works independently.
Three 3 Ω resistors in series have an equivalent resistance of 9 Ω.
Two 4 Ω resistors in parallel have an equivalent resistance of 2 Ω.

quiz.q: Resistors of 5 Ω, 10 Ω and 15 Ω are connected in series. What is the equivalent resistance, in ohms?
quiz.explain: In series, resistances simply add: 5 + 10 + 15 = 30 Ω.
quiz.mistake: Uses the parallel formula for a series circuit

quiz.q: Resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance, in ohms?
quiz.mistake: Adds the resistances as in series

quiz.q: Three resistors of 6 Ω each are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance, in ohms?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 2 instead of 3, or adds them

quiz.q: A 12 V battery is connected to 2 Ω and 4 Ω resistors in series. What current (in amperes) flows?
quiz.mistake: Uses only one resistor

quiz.q: In the same series circuit (2 Ω and 4 Ω, 12 V, 2 A), what is the potential difference (in volts) across the 4 Ω resistor?
quiz.explain: V = IR = 2 × 4 = 8 V. The remaining 4 V is across the 2 Ω resistor.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the voltage is shared equally

quiz.q: Why are household appliances connected in parallel?
options: To make the total resistance very large
So the same current flows through all
So each gets the full voltage and can be switched on or off independently
quiz.explain: Parallel connection gives each appliance the mains voltage and its own current path.
quiz.mistake: Thinks series wiring is used at home

quiz.q: When more resistors are added in parallel, the equivalent resistance —
quiz.explain: Each new branch gives charge another path, so total resistance falls.
quiz.mistake: Expects parallel resistances to add up

quiz.q: Two 10 Ω resistors are connected in parallel across a 5 V cell. What is the current (in amperes) through each resistor?
quiz.explain: Each resistor has 5 V across it: I = 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5 A. Total current is 1 A.
quiz.mistake: Gives the total current instead of the current per branch

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If one bulb goes off in our house, why don't all the others go off too?'
teach.praise: Tweet! House circuits are parallel, so each appliance gets full voltage and works independently!
teach.nudge: Good! But how are home appliances connected — in series or in parallel?

topics.title: Heating effect of current and electric power

learn.hook: Your geyser, iron and toaster all turn electricity into heat — and the electricity bill counts that energy in 'units'!
points: When current flows through a resistor, electrical energy turns into heat. Joule's law of heating: H = I²Rt. Heat produced is proportional to the square of current, to resistance and to time.

Uses: electric iron, toaster, oven, kettle and room heater. In a bulb, the tungsten filament (melting point 3380 °C) glows; bulbs are filled with chemically inactive nitrogen and argon to make the filament last longer.

A fuse is a safety device connected in series. Its wire is an alloy with a suitable melting point; when too much current flows, it melts and breaks the circuit. Home fuses are rated 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A and so on.
Electric power is the rate of using electrical energy: P = VI = I²R = V²/R. Its unit is the watt (1 W = 1 V × 1 A = 1 J/s); 1 kW = 1000 W.
The commercial unit of energy is the kilowatt hour (kWh), the 'unit' on your bill: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

example.q: An electric heater rated 1000 W is used for 2 hours a day. How many units of energy does it use in a day, and what is the cost at ₹6 per unit?
steps: Energy = P × t = 1 kW × 2 h = 2 kWh = 2 units.

learn.reallife: An electric iron rated 1000 W on a 220 V line draws about 4.5 A, so it needs a fuse rated 5 A — this is why fuse ratings matter.

Current in the circuit rises above the fuse rating
Fuse wire heats up quickly
Fuse wire melts
Circuit breaks and current stops

quiz.q: A current of 2 A flows through a 10 Ω resistor for 30 s. How much heat (in joules) is produced?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square the current

quiz.q: What is the power (in watts) of an appliance that draws 5 A from a 220 V supply?
quiz.mistake: Divides voltage by current instead of multiplying

quiz.q: A 1000 W heater is used for 2 hours a day. How many units (kWh) does it use per day?
quiz.explain: Energy = 1 kW × 2 h = 2 kWh.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert watts to kilowatts

quiz.q: If the cost of electricity is ₹6 per unit, what is the cost of using 2 units?
quiz.mistake: Adds instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Why are bulbs filled with nitrogen and argon?
options: These chemically inactive gases prolong the life of the filament
quiz.explain: Inert gases prevent the hot filament from reacting with oxygen and burning out quickly.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the gases create light

quiz.q: How is a fuse connected in a circuit, and why?
options: In series, so it can break the whole circuit when the current is too large
In parallel, so it shares current
In parallel with the earth wire
It is not part of the circuit
quiz.explain: All the current must pass through the fuse; if it melts, the circuit breaks.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a fuse is connected in parallel

quiz.q: A bulb rated 100 W, 220 V. What is its resistance, in ohms?
quiz.mistake: Uses R = V/P or forgets to square V

quiz.q: How many joules are there in 1 kWh?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert hours into seconds

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does Mummy's electric iron get hot? And what does one unit on the electricity bill mean?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Current through resistance makes heat — H = I²Rt — and one unit is one kilowatt hour!
teach.nudge: Good! What is one 'unit' of electricity called in physics?
